transcript.text: GDP Components
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-02
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Calculate consumption, investment, government purchases, and net exports.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

The expenditure approach divides GDP into consumption, investment, government purchases, and net exports. Consumption covers household purchases of final goods and services; investment includes business capital, residential construction, and inventory changes; government purchases pay for current goods and services. Net exports add exports and subtract imports so GDP counts only domestic production, while transfer payments themselves are excluded. A recipient's later purchase is counted separately if it pays for current domestic output.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Classify final spending as consumption, investment, government purchases, or net exports.
Count newly produced capital goods and inventory changes as investment.
Exclude transfer payments because they are not payments for current production.
Subtract imports within net exports so foreign production is not counted in domestic GDP.
WATCH OUT

A common mistake is to count transfer payments as government purchases. Transfers redistribute income and are never themselves part of GDP. A later purchase is classified by what is bought; imports are subtracted in NX.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CLASSIFYING GDP EXPENDITURES

A business buys a newly produced domestic machine for $2 million; this is investment. Government pays contractors $80 million to repair roads; this is government purchases. An $80 million benefit payment is a transfer and is not counted when sent, though any later household purchase of final goods enters consumption. The expenditure identity classifies the counted spending as C + I + G + NX. These purchases contribute $2 million to I and $80 million to G, or $82 million directly to GDP; the transfer is not an additional government purchase.
CHECK YOURSELF
Does a government benefit payment enter G when it is sent?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Real versus Nominal GDP
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-03
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Distinguish nominal and real GDP and calculate the GDP deflator.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Nominal GDP values current production at current prices, while real GDP values it at base-year prices. Multiply current quantities by the designated base-year prices and add across final goods. GDP is a strong measure of market production for its purpose, but it omits some dimensions of welfare. Compare nominal and real GDP to separate price changes from changes in production. Real-GDP growth equals the change in real GDP divided by the initial real GDP.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Nominal GDP uses current-year prices and current-year quantities.
Real GDP uses base-year prices with current-year quantities.
A change in nominal GDP can reflect prices, quantities, or both; a change in real GDP reflects quantities.
Use the GDP deflator to compare nominal GDP with real GDP for the same year.
WATCH OUT
Do not use the new level rather than the initial real-GDP level as the percentage-growth denominator. Real-GDP growth equals the change in real GDP divided by the initial real GDP.
WORKED EXAMPLE: SEPARATING PRICE AND OUTPUT CHANGES

An economy produces 100 units in the base year at $5 each and 110 units this year at $6 each. Nominal GDP this year is 110 x $6 = $660. Real GDP at base-year prices is 110 x $5 = $550. The GDP deflator is ($660 / $550) x 100 = 120, separating the price increase from the output increase.
CHECK YOURSELF
Is real GDP calculated by simply subtracting the inflation rate from nominal GDP?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Limits of GDP
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-04
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Evaluate GDP as a measure of well-being.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

GDP measures market production, not every dimension of well-being. GDP can rise from replacement activity even if people are worse off. GDP is useful, but it is not a complete measure of well-being. Moving activity into or out of markets can change GDP even when useful services or consumer benefit move differently. GDP is useful because income matters, but it leaves out things like leisure, environmental quality, and some nonmarket activity.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
A family replaces unpaid home cooking with otherwise similar restaurant meals.
Unpaid elder care becomes an otherwise similar paid service.
A country has higher GDP, but also more pollution and longer work hours.
A free digital service replaces a paid service while users receive greater benefit.
A free technology replaces paid translation services, measured GDP falls, and users translate more text with less effort.
WATCH OUT

A common mistake is to equate a change in market spending with the same change in total useful services. Moving activity into or out of markets can change GDP even when useful services or consumer benefit move differently.
WORKED EXAMPLE: WHAT GDP MISSES

A hurricane destroys homes, and rebuilding adds $2 billion to measured construction. Holding other domestic production constant, rebuilding adds $2 billion to GDP. It does not subtract the homes that were destroyed or the loss of security and leisure, so the GDP increase does not prove that well-being improved.
CHECK YOURSELF
A hurricane destroys homes, and rebuilding raises measured GDP. Name one loss the GDP increase does not subtract and explain why higher GDP does not prove higher well-being.
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
CPI and Inflation Measurement
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-05
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Calculate CPI and inflation using a market basket.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

The consumer price index compares the current cost of a fixed consumer basket with its base-year cost. The index equals the current basket cost divided by the base-year basket cost, multiplied by one hundred. Inflation is the percentage change in the index between periods. Holding basket quantities fixed isolates price change from changes in what consumers buy.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Identify the fixed basket, its base-year cost, and its current-year cost.
Compute the price index by comparing the current basket cost with the base-year basket cost.
Measure inflation as the percentage change in the index from one period to the next.
Keep basket quantities fixed when calculating the CPI for different years.
WATCH OUT
Do not use the wrong basket cost or forget to multiply by 100. Divide the current cost of the fixed basket by its base-year cost; the index can rise or fall as prices change.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CALCULATING CPI AND INFLATION

The fixed basket costs $80 in the base year and $98 now. CPI = ($98 / $80) x 100 = 122.5. Relative to the base-year index of 100, prices rose 22.5%. Separately, an index rising from 125 to 150 implies inflation of (150 - 125) / 125 x 100 = 20%.
CHECK YOURSELF
A basket costs $400 in the base year and $500 today. What is today's CPI?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
CPI Bias
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-06
Time: 4 minutes
Outcome: Analyze substitution, quality, and new-goods bias.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A fixed-basket index can overstate growth in the cost of maintaining a living standard when buyers substitute toward relatively cheaper goods. Quality improvements and new goods also complicate price comparisons. These issues distinguish a change in posted prices from a change in the cost of obtaining comparable benefits.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
If goods improve in quality, price increases may overstate the rise in the cost of living.
If consumers substitute, their actual cost of living may rise less than the fixed basket suggests.
A new product gives consumers a useful option that did not previously exist.
A product becomes more expensive but also much higher quality.
A laptop price rises while speed and battery life improve.
WATCH OUT
Do not treat all price increases as inflation even when quality or product variety improves. If goods improve in quality, price increases may overstate the rise in the cost of living.
WORKED EXAMPLE: RECOGNIZING CPI BIAS

A fixed basket contains beef even after beef prices rise sharply. Consumers substitute toward chicken, but the CPI continues pricing the original beef quantity. Because the fixed basket misses that cost-saving response, measured inflation can exceed the increase in the cost of maintaining consumers' actual purchasing pattern.
CHECK YOURSELF
A refrigerator sells for the same price but uses much less electricity and lasts longer. Which CPI issue matters?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
CPI versus GDP Deflator
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-07
Time: 4 minutes
Outcome: Compare the construction and uses of CPI and the GDP deflator.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

The CPI tracks prices paid for a consumer basket, while the GDP deflator tracks prices of currently produced domestic final output. Imported consumer goods affect CPI but not the GDP deflator directly. Use CPI for consumer purchasing-power questions and the GDP deflator for the price level of current domestic GDP. Identify the buyer and production location, then match the price change to the index whose scope includes it. CPI follows a consumer-basket framework; the GDP deflator follows prices of current domestically produced final output.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Use CPI for consumer purchasing-power questions and the GDP deflator for the price level of current domestic GDP.
A domestic firm buys newly produced business software whose price rises.
Imported prescription-drug prices rise while prices of domestic hospital services are unchanged.
A city buys domestic transit vehicles while households buy imported fuel.
Domestic food-export prices rise and imported-clothing prices fall.
WATCH OUT

Do not treat CPI and the GDP deflator as interchangeable measures of the same set of prices. CPI follows a consumer-basket framework; the GDP deflator follows prices of current domestically produced final output.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CHOOSING THE RIGHT PRICE INDEX

The price of imported coffee rises while prices of domestically produced goods are unchanged. Coffee is in the consumer basket, so the increase can raise CPI. Because the coffee was produced abroad, it is not part of domestic GDP and does not directly raise the GDP deflator.
CHECK YOURSELF
Which price index uses a fixed basket of consumer goods?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Indexing and Real Values
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-08
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Convert nominal values across time and apply indexation.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A price index converts nominal amounts across time and can be used to index wages, benefits, rents, or tax thresholds. Converting an earlier nominal amount into later dollars requires multiplying by the later index divided by the earlier index. Indexation preserves purchasing power only when the chosen index and adjustment timing closely match the prices relevant to the recipient.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Identify the nominal amount, the starting index, and the ending index.
Scale the nominal amount by the ratio of the ending index to the starting index.
Check whether the contract uses the same index and adjustment timing as the prices relevant to the recipient.
A fully indexed nominal payment preserves purchasing power only to the extent that the index matches actual costs.
WATCH OUT

Do not assume an indexed contract guarantees an exact real outcome in every circumstance. Indexation adjusts a nominal amount using a specified index; lags or an imperfectly matched index can still change real value.
WORKED EXAMPLE: INDEXING A NOMINAL PAYMENT

A salary was $40,000 when CPI was 100. CPI is now 160. 40,000 x 160/100 = 64,000.  Indexation adjusts a nominal amount using a specified index; lags or an imperfectly matched index can still change real value.
CHECK YOURSELF
Why might a tax threshold be indexed to a price index?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Living Standards and Growth
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-10
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Use real GDP per person and compounding to compare living standards.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Real GDP per person is a common measure of material living standards, and compounding makes sustained growth powerful over time. Dividing real output by population distinguishes growth in total production from growth in average material resources. Productivity growth can raise output per person without requiring proportionally more work, although this measure does not capture every dimension of well-being.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
A country raises output mainly by requiring much longer workweeks, while output per hour is unchanged.
Higher productivity lets an economy produce more goods and services from its available labor and resources.
Real GDP per person is commonly used to compare living standards and growth.
Real GDP per person relates inflation-adjusted output to the number of people sharing that output.
Compare growth in real GDP with population growth to distinguish total output from output per person.
WATCH OUT

A common mistake is to equate more total labor input with higher productivity or complete welfare improvement. Productivity is output per unit of input, and GDP omits important dimensions of well-being.
WORKED EXAMPLE: COMPOUNDING LIVING-STANDARD GROWTH

If real GDP per person grows at 4% per year, the Rule of 70 estimates a doubling time of 70/4 = 17.5 years. This calculation describes material output growth, not complete well-being: longer work hours can raise GDP per person without raising output per hour or preserving leisure.
CHECK YOURSELF
Country A grows at 2% per year and Country B at 4%. Use the Rule of 70 to compare approximate doubling times. Why does a small growth-rate difference matter over decades?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Unemployment Measurement
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-14
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Classify labor-force status and calculate unemployment and participation rates.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Labor-force status depends on work, job attachment, availability, and active job search. Employed people include those working for pay or profit, those temporarily absent from a job, and qualifying unpaid family workers. Unemployed people have no job, are available, and actively searched in the past four weeks; people awaiting recall from temporary layoff need not search. Discouraged workers who have stopped searching are outside the labor force.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Work for pay or profit during the reference week counts as employment, even if part-time.
At least 15 hours of unpaid work in a family business also counts as employment.
Labor force = employed + unemployed; unemployment rate = unemployed / labor force x 100.
Participation rate = labor force / civilian noninstitutional population age 16 and older x 100.
WATCH OUT
Wanting a job alone does not make a person unemployed. Check job status, availability, and active search, including the temporary-layoff exception. Discouraged workers are outside the labor force.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CLASSIFYING LABOR-FORCE STATUS

Among 100 people in the civilian noninstitutional population age 16 and older, 60 are employed, 5 are unemployed, and 35 are outside the labor force. Labor force = 60 + 5 = 65. Unemployment rate = 5/65 x 100 = 7.7%; participation rate = 65/100 x 100 = 65%.
CHECK YOURSELF
Which two groups are added to calculate the labor force?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Types of Unemployment
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-15
Time: 4 minutes
Outcome: Distinguish frictional, structural, and cyclical unemployment.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Frictional unemployment comes from ordinary job search, structural unemployment from lasting mismatches, and cyclical unemployment from recessions. Layoffs caused by recession are cyclical unemployment. Short-term search between jobs is frictional unemployment. Job loss from weak demand during a recession is cyclical unemployment. A long-term mismatch between skills and available jobs is structural unemployment.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
A worker loses a job because a recession causes customers to spend less.
A coal miner loses work because the economy shifts permanently toward other energy sources and the miner lacks transferable skills.
Frictional unemployment exists because workers and firms take time to match.
Structural unemployment is about mismatch; frictional unemployment is about normal search.
A college graduate takes two months to find a first job that matches their skills.
WATCH OUT

Do not confuse the cause of unemployment with official labor-force status. For a jobless worker who is available and actively searching, normal search after leaving a job is frictional unemployment; recession-related job loss is cyclical unemployment.
WORKED EXAMPLE: IDENTIFYING UNEMPLOYMENT TYPES

A worker leaves a job and spends six weeks searching for a better match; that is frictional unemployment. A factory worker whose skills no longer match available technology faces structural unemployment. A restaurant worker laid off because a recession reduces spending experiences cyclical unemployment.
CHECK YOURSELF
A worker's occupation disappears after a lasting technology change, and their skills do not match new vacancies. Which type of unemployment is this, and how does it differ from ordinary job search?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Money Functions and Measures
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-18
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Identify money's functions, forms, and M1/M2 measurement.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Money serves as a medium of exchange, a unit of account, and a store of value. As a medium of exchange it facilitates purchases; as a unit of account it provides a common way to quote prices and debts; as a store of value it carries purchasing power into the future. Money-supply measures group liquid assets by how readily they can perform these functions.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
A medium of exchange is used to buy and sell goods and services.
A unit of account provides the common measure in which prices and debts are stated.
A store of value transfers purchasing power from the present into the future.
For a money-supply measure, classify an asset by its liquidity and the measure's stated definition.
WATCH OUT

A transfer from a checking deposit to a retail money-market fund lowers M1 but leaves M2 unchanged. Checking and savings deposits are included in both under the stated post-2020 definition; retail money-market funds are only in M2.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CLASSIFYING MONEY-SUPPLY MEASURES

Currency is $800, checking deposits are $1,200, and savings deposits are $1,500. Under the U.S. definition used since May 2020, savings deposits are included in M1, so M1 = $3,500. With no other M2 components, M2 is also $3,500. Under the older textbook definition excluding savings from M1, M1 would be $2,000.
CHECK YOURSELF
Are retail money-market mutual funds included in M1, M2, or both?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Central Banking and the Federal Reserve
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-19
Time: 4 minutes
Outcome: Explain central-bank structure, roles, independence, and the FOMC.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

The Federal Reserve conducts monetary policy, supplies reserve balances, supports payments, and serves as lender of last resort. Its structure includes the Board of Governors and 12 regional Reserve Banks; the FOMC directs monetary policy. Operational independence allows policy decisions without day-to-day political approval within a mandate set by Congress. The Treasury manages federal finances rather than monetary policy.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
The Federal Reserve conducts monetary policy and supports the banking/payments system; the Treasury manages federal finances and debt operations.
The FOMC sets the monetary-policy stance and directs open-market operations.
A central-bank committee decides to change monetary conditions.
A commercial bank approves a loan and credits the borrower’s checking account.
Commercial banks create deposit liabilities when they lend; the central bank creates reserve balances/base money used by banks.
WATCH OUT

Do not treat commercial-bank deposits and central-bank reserves as the same liability issued by the same institution. Commercial banks create deposit liabilities when they lend; the central bank creates reserve balances/base money used by banks.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CENTRAL BANK OR TREASURY?

The Federal Reserve buys Treasury securities from a bank, adding reserve balances. In the limited-reserves textbook model, this tends to lower short-term rates; in an ample-reserves system, administered rates are the main rate-control tool. The purchase is monetary policy, not a change in federal taxes or spending.
CHECK YOURSELF
Which group directs open-market operations?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Monetary-Policy Tools
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-21
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Apply open-market operations, administered rates, and reserve tools.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

The Federal Reserve influences bank reserves, the money supply, and short-term interest rates through several policy tools. Open-market purchases add reserves to the banking system, while open-market sales remove them. Administered rates change the incentives banks face when borrowing or holding reserves. Changes in reserves can affect bank lending and deposit creation, although the actual expansion of money may be smaller than the simple textbook multiplier predicts.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
An open-market purchase adds reserves; in the limited-reserves model this tends to lower short-term rates.
An open-market sale removes reserves; in the limited-reserves model this tends to raise short-term rates.
Lower administered rates ease monetary conditions; higher administered rates restrain them.
In an ample-reserves system, administered rates are the main tool for controlling short-term rates.
WATCH OUT
More reserves do not guarantee a fixed expansion of broad money. Banks, borrowers, and depositors affect the response; the simple multiplier is a separate restrictive model.
WORKED EXAMPLE: MATCHING THE TOOL TO ITS EFFECT

A $50 million security purchase adds $50 million of reserves. In a limited-reserves textbook market, that tends to lower short-term interest rates. In an ample-reserves system, administered rates are the main rate-control tool. Distinguish each tool's immediate effect from the eventual lending and spending response.
CHECK YOURSELF
If the central bank lowers the rate it charges banks for direct loans, what is the immediate textbook effect?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Limits of Monetary Control
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-22
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Evaluate currency drain, excess reserves, leverage risk, and multiplier slippage.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

The central bank influences broad money, but banks and the public also determine lending, deposits, and currency holdings. Excess reserve holding and currency drain weaken the simple deposit-expansion process. Banks with little capital may be especially cautious about losses and lending. These choices prevent a mechanical link from new reserves to a fixed amount of broad money.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
The Fed influences the money supply, but banks and depositors affect reserves, lending, and deposits.
When banks hold more excess reserves, they lend less, so deposit creation weakens.
The Fed can influence money creation, but banks and the public also matter.
The central bank adds reserves, but banks choose to hold much of them as excess reserves.
Households convert part of each new bank deposit into currency rather than leaving the funds in banks.
WATCH OUT

Do not treat the central bank as having mechanical one-for-one control over broad money. The central bank controls its own balance sheet and reserve conditions more directly than broad money, which also depends on banks, borrowers, and the public.
WORKED EXAMPLE: WHY MONEY EXPANSION FALLS SHORT

The Fed adds $40 million of reserves, but banks hold half as excess reserves and the public keeps some funds as cash. Because only part of the injection supports new loans and redeposits, broad money rises by less than the simple multiplier predicts. The Fed controls reserves more directly than it controls deposits held by the public. A bank with a thin capital cushion may also limit new lending to reduce its exposure to losses.
CHECK YOURSELF
Why is Fed control of the money supply imperfect?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Monetary Neutrality
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-24
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Distinguish nominal and real variables and analyze long-run neutrality.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Monetary neutrality means that a lasting change in the money supply changes nominal variables but not real output or employment in the long run. Nominal variables changed, but real output did not. Monetary neutrality means nominal variables can change without changing real variables in the long run. Separate nominal from real variables. A proportional change in nominal wages and prices can leave purchasing power unchanged.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Separate nominal variables, measured in money, from real variables, measured in goods, services, or purchasing power.
A lasting money-supply change can alter the price level and other nominal values in the long run.
Under monetary neutrality, long-run real output and employment remain determined by real resources and technology.
Do not apply long-run neutrality to the short run, when sticky prices can make money affect real activity.
WATCH OUT
Do not assume money changes real variables permanently in the long run. Monetary neutrality means money affects nominal variables in the long run, not real output or employment.
WORKED EXAMPLE: NOMINAL VERSUS REAL EFFECTS

Under the stated long-run neutrality assumptions, doubling money doubles prices and nominal wages. The real wage is unchanged: $20 / $5 = 4 units per hour before and $40 / $10 = 4 afterward. Real output remains 100 units. Nominal amounts change while real purchasing power and productive capacity do not.
CHECK YOURSELF
A student says, “If money is neutral, monetary policy can never affect real output.” What is the best correction?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Costs of Inflation
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-26
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Analyze redistribution, shoeleather costs, menu costs, and price distortions.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Unexpected inflation redistributes purchasing power between borrowers and lenders on fixed nominal contracts. Even expected inflation can create costs: changing posted prices uses resources (menu costs), economizing on cash takes time and effort (shoeleather costs), and uneven price changes can obscure relative-price signals.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Unexpected inflation lowers the real repayment on a fixed nominal debt.
Menu costs are resources spent changing posted prices.
Shoeleather costs arise from efforts to hold less money during inflation.
Relative-price confusion can make economic decisions harder.
WATCH OUT
Do not confuse shoeleather costs with menu costs. Shoeleather costs are the wasted effort people spend trying to hold less money during inflation.
WORKED EXAMPLE: UNEXPECTED INFLATION REDISTRIBUTION

A lender makes a 9% loan expecting 3% inflation, so the expected real return is approximately 6%. Actual inflation turns out to be 10%, making the realized real return approximately 9% - 10% = -1%. Unexpected inflation transfers purchasing power from the lender to the borrower.
CHECK YOURSELF
A student says, “If everyone correctly expects 6 percent inflation, inflation has no economic costs.” Which response is best?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Fiscal Policy and Aggregate Demand
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-30
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Trace government purchases and taxes into aggregate demand.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Fiscal policy shifts aggregate demand through changes in government purchases, taxes, and their effects on consumption. Lower purchases and higher taxes both push aggregate demand left. After the first-round spending change, the multiplier process traces additional income-consumption rounds; crowding out can then reduce the net effect. A tax cut raises disposable income, which can increase consumption and shift AD right.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Higher government purchases directly raise aggregate demand; lower purchases reduce it.
Tax changes affect aggregate demand indirectly by changing disposable income and consumption.
Expansionary fiscal policy shifts aggregate demand right; contractionary policy shifts it left.
Distinguish a shift of aggregate demand from a movement along the curve caused by the price level.
WATCH OUT

A common mistake is to classify fiscal policy from the economy's condition rather than the government's action. Higher purchases or lower taxes are expansionary; lower purchases or higher taxes are contractionary.
WORKED EXAMPLE: SHIFTING AGGREGATE DEMAND

Price level vertical and real output demanded horizontal. AD2 lies right of AD1. At the same price level P, quantity demanded rises from Y1 to Y2 after expansionary fiscal action. Only two AD curves are shown; the graph does not determine the new AD-AS equilibrium or a multiplier magnitude.

At the displayed price level P, higher government purchases shift aggregate demand from AD1 to AD2. Real output demanded rises from Y1 to Y2 at that fixed price level. A tax cut can also shift AD right by raising disposable income and consumption. This graph isolates the direction of the shift; the multiplier and offsets are considered separately.
CHECK YOURSELF
Why can a tax cut shift aggregate demand to the right in the short run?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Long-Run Phillips Curve
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-38
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Apply the natural-rate hypothesis and vertical long-run Phillips curve.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

The long-run Phillips curve is vertical at the natural unemployment rate because expected inflation eventually adjusts. A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate. Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate. The long-run Phillips curve is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
The long-run Phillips curve is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment.
Expected inflation rises from 2 percent to 5 percent while unemployment remains at its natural rate.
The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.
A national job-matching system reduces the time workers spend searching for suitable positions.
WATCH OUT

Do not treat a higher expected inflation rate as a permanent way to lower unemployment. Along the long-run Phillips curve, different inflation rates can coexist with the same natural rate of unemployment.
WORKED EXAMPLE: RETURNING TO THE NATURAL RATE

Unemployment horizontal, inflation vertical. LRPC is vertical at 5 percent unemployment. Initial A on SRPC0 is (5,3). Demand expansion moves along SRPC0 to B (3,5). Expected inflation adjustment shifts SRPC up to SRPC1; final C (5,5) is at its intersection with LRPC. Arrows show A to B to C.

The economy starts at A: 5% unemployment and 3% inflation. A demand expansion moves it along SRPC0 to B, at 3% unemployment and 5% inflation. As expected inflation rises, SRPC shifts up to SRPC1. The final point C is on LRPC at 5% unemployment and 5% inflation. Unemployment returns to its natural rate; there is no permanent inflation-unemployment tradeoff.
CHECK YOURSELF
Why does higher inflation not permanently lower unemployment in the natural-rate model?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Sacrifice Ratio
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-41
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Calculate and interpret output losses associated with disinflation.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output lost for each percentage-point reduction in inflation. Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment. The preferred path depends on credibility, expectations, adjustment speed, uncertainty, and cumulative costs. The sacrifice ratio measures how much output is lost when inflation is reduced. If expected inflation falls faster, the short-run cost of disinflation can be smaller.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
The sacrifice ratio measures how much output is lost when inflation is reduced.
If expected inflation falls faster, the short-run cost of disinflation can be smaller.
The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.
A disinflation has a lower sacrifice ratio than another.
Faster adjustment of expected inflation reduces the output cost of disinflation.
WATCH OUT

A common mistake is to divide the dollar output loss directly by the inflation change. First express the loss as a percentage of potential output, then divide by the percentage-point reduction in inflation.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CALCULATING THE SACRIFICE RATIO

Each year loses $12 billion relative to $400 billion potential output, a 3% gap. Add the two annual gaps: cumulative loss is 6% of one year's potential output. Inflation falls by 3 percentage points, so the sacrifice ratio is 6 / 3 = 2. Keep percentage output losses distinct from percentage-point inflation changes.
CHECK YOURSELF
Should annual output gaps be added before calculating a multi-year sacrifice ratio?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Saving, Investment, and National-Saving Identities
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-42
Time: 6 minutes
Outcome: Calculate private, public, and national saving in closed and open economies.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

With net taxes T, private saving is Y - T - C and public saving is T - G. National saving is their sum: S = Y - C - G. In a closed economy, S = I. In an open economy, S = I + NCO; because NX = NCO in the course model, S = I + NX. These are aggregate identities, not claims that each saver directly funds one investor.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Budget surplus means T - G is positive; a deficit makes public saving negative.
Adding private and public saving cancels T and gives Y - C - G.
Use S = I only for the closed-economy model.
In an open economy, saving can finance domestic investment or net capital outflow.
WATCH OUT
Do not reverse the public-saving sign. T - G is public saving; G - T is the budget deficit. Also state the closed-economy assumption before writing S = I.
WORKED EXAMPLE: FROM COMPONENTS TO OPEN-ECONOMY SAVING

Let Y = $1,200, T = $150, C = $760, and G = $260. Private saving is $290; public saving is -$110; national saving is $180. If domestic investment is $140, then NCO = S - I = $40. The accounting identity also gives NX = $40.
CHECK YOURSELF
Private saving is $220 and public saving is -$50. What is national saving?

Deficits, Debt, and Government Borrowing
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-47
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Distinguish annual budget flows from accumulated public debt.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A budget deficit occurs when government outlays exceed revenues during a period; it is financed by borrowing and tends to add to public debt. A surplus can reduce debt if used for repayment. Debt is the accumulated stock of outstanding borrowing, not the current year's deficit. Borrowing can finance valuable investment or current spending, so its effects depend on use, scale, interest costs, and economic conditions.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Deficit: one period's negative budget balance; debt: outstanding stock at a date.
New borrowing generally rises with a deficit and adds to debt.
Interest payments can absorb future budget resources.
Lower public saving links deficits to loanable funds and possible crowding out.
WATCH OUT

Debt is a stock, not this year's deficit or the sum of all past spending. When a deficit is measured using total outlays, interest is already included: do not add it again when updating debt. Other accounting adjustments may also matter.
WORKED EXAMPLE: UPDATING THE DEBT STOCK

Public debt begins at $900 billion. A $120 billion deficit adds borrowing; the next year's $20 billion surplus is used to repay debt. Ignoring other adjustments, debt becomes $900 + $120 - $20 = $1,000 billion. The two annual balances are flows; $1,000 billion is the ending stock.
CHECK YOURSELF
Can the debt remain positive in a year with a budget surplus? Explain briefly.

Debt Measures, Debt Burden, and Fiscal Data
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-48
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Interpret debt levels, debt-to-GDP ratios, and interest burdens.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

The debt level is a nominal dollar stock; the debt-to-GDP ratio compares that stock with the economy's annual income and productive capacity. Ratios support comparisons across time and economies, but they do not by themselves prove sustainability. Interest rates, economic growth, revenues, primary balances, maturity, and investor confidence also matter at a Principles level.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Debt-to-GDP = public debt divided by nominal GDP, multiplied by 100 percent.
Debt can rise while debt-to-GDP falls if nominal GDP grows faster.
Interest burden can be compared with GDP, revenue, or total outlays.
Nominal levels answer size questions; ratios answer size-relative-to-capacity questions.
WATCH OUT
Do not interpret one ratio as a mechanical crisis threshold. Use consistent definitions and dates, then combine the ratio with growth, interest costs, and budget information.
WORKED EXAMPLE: LEVEL UP, RATIO DOWN

Debt rises from $6.0 trillion to $6.6 trillion while nominal GDP rises from $24.0 trillion to $27.5 trillion. Debt-to-GDP moves from 25.0% to 24.0%. The debt level increased, but the economy's nominal scale grew faster, so the relative measure fell.
CHECK YOURSELF
Debt is $9 trillion and nominal GDP is $30 trillion. What is the debt-to-GDP ratio?

Deposit Creation and the Money Multiplier
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-49
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Apply the textbook fractional-reserve deposit-creation process.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

In the simple textbook model, banks keep the required fraction of deposits as reserves and lend the rest. When loan proceeds are redeposited, another bank can lend part again. The repeated process creates deposits. The simple money multiplier m = 1 / rr gives the theoretical maximum total deposit expansion per dollar of new reserves under full lending and redepositing.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Required reserves = reserve ratio x deposits; excess reserves can support new lending.
A lower reserve ratio produces a larger simple multiplier.
Each lending round is smaller because a fraction is retained as reserves.
Currency holding and excess reserves make actual expansion smaller than the maximum.
WATCH OUT
Do not confuse the multiplier with bank capital or claim that one bank lends the entire multiplied amount. The multiplier summarizes repeated system-wide rounds under restrictive assumptions.
WORKED EXAMPLE: A THEORETICAL MAXIMUM

With rr = 10%, the simple multiplier is 1 / 0.10 = 10. If $1,000 of new reserves enters the banking system, maximum total deposits are $10,000. Banks collectively retain $1,000 as required reserves and can support up to $9,000 of new loans. Cash holding or excess reserves lowers the result.
CHECK YOURSELF
If rr rises from 10% to 20%, what happens to the simple multiplier?

International Transactions and Open-Economy Identities
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-52
Time: 6 minutes
Outcome: Calculate trade and capital balances and connect NX, NCO, saving, and investment.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Net exports are exports minus imports: NX = X - M. Positive NX is a trade surplus; negative NX is a trade deficit. Net capital outflow is domestic purchases of foreign assets minus foreign purchases of domestic assets. In the course accounting model, NX = NCO. National saving finances domestic investment and NCO, so S = I + NCO = I + NX.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Exports add to NX; imports subtract from NX.
A domestic resident buying a foreign asset raises capital outflow and NCO.
A foreign resident buying a domestic asset lowers NCO and is a capital inflow.
If S exceeds I, the difference is positive NCO and positive NX.
WATCH OUT
Do not import Micro tariff or comparative-advantage analysis into these identities. Also do not call a trade deficit a mathematical error: it corresponds to negative NCO in the accounting model.
WORKED EXAMPLE: MATCHING THE TWO SIDES

Exports are $300 billion and imports are $360 billion, so NX = -$60 billion. Residents buy $90 billion of foreign assets while foreigners buy $150 billion of domestic assets, so NCO = $90 - $150 = -$60 billion. If investment is $240 billion, saving is I + NCO = $180 billion.
CHECK YOURSELF
National saving is $250 billion and investment is $210 billion. What are NCO and NX?

Capital Flows and Net Capital Outflow
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-55
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Classify international asset purchases and trace interest-rate effects on NCO.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Net capital outflow equals domestic residents' purchases of foreign assets minus foreign residents' purchases of domestic assets. Positive NCO is net capital outflow; negative NCO is net capital inflow. Capital tends to move toward more attractive risk-adjusted returns. In the textbook model, a higher domestic real interest rate lowers NCO and therefore reduces the supply of dollars in the foreign-exchange market.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
A U.S. resident buying a foreign bond raises U.S. NCO.
A foreign resident buying a U.S. asset lowers U.S. NCO.
Higher domestic real returns attract inflow and discourage outflow, lowering NCO.
NCO supplies dollars to the FX market as residents acquire foreign assets.
WATCH OUT
NCO and NX describe different transactions: assets versus goods and services. They are equal as an accounting relationship in the course model, not because every asset purchase is an export.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CLASSIFY, THEN NET

Initially residents buy $140 billion of foreign assets and foreigners buy $90 billion of domestic assets, giving NCO of $50 billion. Suppose a higher domestic real interest rate makes domestic assets more attractive: residents' foreign purchases fall to $130 billion and foreigners' domestic purchases rise to $100 billion. NCO falls to $30 billion. These illustrative flows show the direction; the model does not predict a fixed response size.
CHECK YOURSELF
Foreign purchases of U.S. assets rise while U.S. foreign-asset purchases are fixed. What happens to U.S. NCO?
